Chapter 4: Creating Space Between Self and Emotions
Now that you've started noticing and naming your emotions, there's an important next step—learning how to create a little distance from them.
And no, this isn’t about pushing feelings away or pretending they don’t exist. It’s more like realizing that emotions are just experiences you go through, not labels that define who you are or what your future holds.
Have you ever caught yourself thinking, “I am anxious” or “I am a failure,” and started to believe that’s the full story of who you are?
When we get fused with our thoughts and feelings like that, it’s easy to fall into rigid patterns—reacting to each emotion as if it’s in charge, instead of making choices that really fit our long-term values.
Imagine you’re standing so close to a painting that all you can see is a single brushstroke. But when you step back, you get to see the whole masterpiece.
That’s what creating space from your emotions is like. It opens up room to see the bigger picture, giving you more freedom in how you respond.
One super helpful way to do this is by shifting the language you use with yourself.
Instead of saying, “I am angry,” try, “I notice that I’m feeling anger.”
It sounds simple, but this small change can gently remind you that emotions are just passing states—they don’t define you.
Here’s another idea: picture your thoughts and feelings as clouds drifting across the sky.
Sometimes they’re heavy and dark, sometimes light and barely there, but they always move on.
By watching them come and go, you give yourself permission to respond with more wisdom and care, rather than getting swept away.
Want some practical ways to put this into action?
Try using phrases like, “I’m noticing the thought that…” or “I’m having the feeling of…”
Or, visualize your emotions as waves, clouds, or even passing cars—here one moment, gone the next.
And, if you need an anchor, just come back to your breath. Focusing on mindful breathing lets emotions rise and fade without getting caught up in judgment.
This whole process is often called “defusion.”
It’s about breaking that automatic link between what you feel and what you do.
For example, just because you’re angry doesn’t mean you have to lash out.
Feeling anxious? It doesn’t have to stop you from taking on a new challenge.
Let’s look at what this might look like in real life.
Picture a parent who feels frustration bubbling up during a child’s tantrum.
Instead of reacting in the heat of the moment, they pause, notice the feeling, take a breath, and choose patience.
Or, imagine a professional facing self-doubt before a big presentation.
The anxiety is real, but instead of letting it take over, they acknowledge it and move forward anyway, driven by a deeper commitment to growth.
Over time, this ability to step back from emotions builds true resilience and flexibility.
It lets you act with greater freedom—even when things feel uncomfortable or uncertain.
And in the middle of life’s changes, when old habits aren’t working anymore, this skill can really make all the difference.
So, by practicing how to observe your emotions without getting tangled up in them, you’ll find it easier to handle life’s ups and downs—with more ease, and a lot more confidence.
And that sets the stage for what comes next: discovering how to connect with your core values, and let them guide your actions.
